---
title: "Module 4 — KL divergence and Bregman geometry"
---

## Overview

**Why this module exists.** Every approximate inference method in this workshop replaces
a posterior you cannot compute with a distribution you can. To do that honestly you
need a number that says how far the approximation is from the truth, and you need to be
able to compute that number, or at least its gradient, without ever touching the
intractable posterior. The Kullback–Leibler divergence is that number. This module
builds it from first principles, shows that for exponential families it collapses to a
formula involving only the log-partition function $A$ of Module 3, and then uses the
same convex geometry to invert the mean map and to define the natural gradient. Day 2
will minimise KL; this module is where you learn what you are minimising.

**What you'll build:** in `workshop/m04_kl_bregman.py`, a single closed-form KL
divergence that works for every family in Module 3, a Monte Carlo KL to validate it,
hand-written textbook KL formulas that must agree with it, a Newton inversion from mean
parameters back to natural parameters, the convex conjugate $A^*$, and the natural
gradient. These are the tools CAVI (Module 6), stochastic variational inference (Module
8) and the conjugate updates of Module 5 are built from.

**Estimated time:** 2.5 hours (about 1 hour reading, 1.5 hours building).

**Prerequisites:** [Module 3](m03-expfam-core.qmd),
[Module 2b](../day0/m02b-foundations.qmd) for what a posterior is and why we
approximate it. Terms are defined in the [glossary](../reference/glossary.qmd).

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

1. State what $\KL(p\,\|\,q)$ measures in two different readings (wasted code length
   and expected log-likelihood ratio), prove it is non-negative, and explain with a
   numerical example why it is not symmetric.
2. Derive $\KL(p_{\eta_p}\,\|\,p_{\eta_q})$ as the Bregman divergence of $A$ and compute
   it for any family from `log_partition` and `mean_params` alone.
3. Invert the mean map $\mu = \nabla A(\eta)$ numerically and explain why Newton's
   method with the Fisher matrix is the right algorithm and why it needs damping.
4. Read the convex conjugate $A^*(\mu) = \eta^\top\mu - A(\eta)$ off a picture of $A$
   and its tangent line, identify $A^*$ as negative entropy, and verify
   $\nabla A^* = \eta$ by autodiff.
5. (Optional Step 4.) Explain why "steepest descent" depends on how you measure
   distance, compute a natural gradient, and show it equals the ordinary gradient in
   mean coordinates.

## Background

### The problem in plain terms

In [Module 2b](../day0/m02b-foundations.qmd) you saw that the posterior is defined but
usually not computable, and that the two ways out are to sample from it (Day 3) or to
pick the closest member of a family of tractable distributions (Day 2). "Closest" needs
a definition. It must be computable from things we have (the unnormalised posterior and
the candidate $q$), it must be zero only when the two distributions agree, and its
gradient with respect to the parameters of $q$ must be something we can estimate. The
divergence that satisfies all three is the KL divergence, and the reason it is
computable for the families of Module 3 is that it is a function of $A$ alone.

A second, more practical problem appears in the same breath. Module 3 gave you the map
from natural parameters to mean parameters, $\mu = \nabla A(\eta)$. Algorithms often hand
you the other direction: an update produces expected sufficient statistics (a mean and a
second moment, say) and you need the natural parameters that have them. That inverse is
not available in closed form for most families, so you build a solver for it here.

### Definitions

**Divergence.** A function $D(p, q) \ge 0$ of two distributions with $D(p, q) = 0$ if and
only if $p = q$. It need not be symmetric and need not satisfy the triangle inequality;
a divergence is not a distance. "Divergence" is the right word precisely because these
properties are missing.

**Kullback–Leibler divergence.** For densities $p$ and $q$ on the same space,

$$
\KL(p\,\|\,q) = \E_{x\sim p}\big[\log p(x) - \log q(x)\big] = \int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\dd x.
$$

Read it as: *average, under $p$, of the log-likelihood ratio of $p$ to $q$*. The
expectation is taken under the first argument. Two readings make it concrete.

- **Coding.** If you build an optimal compressor for data from $q$ but the data actually
  come from $p$, you pay on average $\KL(p\,\|\,q)$ extra nats per symbol compared with a
  compressor built for $p$. KL is wasted code length. A nat is the unit when logs are
  natural; divide by $\log 2$ for bits.
- **Testing.** If you observe $n$ samples and want to decide whether they came from $p$
  or $q$, the log-likelihood ratio $\sum_i \log\frac{p(x_i)}{q(x_i)}$ grows like
  $n\,\KL(p\,\|\,q)$ when $p$ is true. KL is the rate at which evidence accumulates. To
  reach a false-negative rate $\alpha$ you need roughly $n \approx \log(1/\alpha)/\KL(p\,\|\,q)$
  samples (this is the Chernoff–Stein lemma).

**Entropy.** $H(p) = -\E_p[\log p(x)]$, the average code length of an optimal compressor
for $p$, and the quantity whose negative turns out to be the convex conjugate of $A$.

**Bregman divergence.** For a convex function $F$, $D_F(a, b) = F(a) - F(b) - (a-b)^\top\nabla F(b)$:
the value of $F$ at $a$ minus the value of the tangent plane at $b$, evaluated at $a$.
Convexity says the function lies above every tangent plane, so $D_F \ge 0$.

### KL is non-negative, in three lines

Write $\KL(p\,\|\,q) = -\E_p\big[\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\big]$. Since $\log$ is concave,
Jensen's inequality (question 1 of the diagnostic) gives
$\E_p[\log u] \le \log\E_p[u]$ for any positive random variable $u$. With
$u = q(x)/p(x)$,

$$
\E_p\Big[\log\frac{q}{p}\Big] \le \log\E_p\Big[\frac{q}{p}\Big] = \log\int p(x)\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\dd x = \log 1 = 0,
$$

so $\KL(p\,\|\,q) \ge 0$. Equality in Jensen holds only when $u$ is constant, that is
when $q = p$ almost everywhere.

### Asymmetry, with numbers

Take $p = \mathcal N(0, 1)$ and $q = \mathcal N(0, 3^2)$.

**Predict before reading on.** One of $\KL(p\,\|\,q)$ and $\KL(q\,\|\,p)$ is about four
times the other. Which, and why? Decide before opening the answer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The univariate formula (Module 2, Step 4) gives

$$
\KL(\mathcal N(0,1)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,9)) = 0.654, \qquad
\KL(\mathcal N(0,9)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,1)) = 2.901.
$$

The expensive direction is the one where the samples come from the *wide*
distribution and are scored by the narrow one. The reasoning is in the next paragraph;
the figure below shows the two integrands.
:::

![The integrand of each KL direction. Left: samples from the narrow $p$ scored by the wide $q$; the penalty is spread thinly and sums to $0.654$. Right: samples from the wide distribution scored by the narrow one; the tails at $|x| > 2$ are punished quadratically and the total is $2.901$.](../figures/m04_kl_asymmetry.png)

Why so different? In the first case the samples come from the narrow distribution and
are scored by the wide one: every sample lands where $q$ has reasonable density, so the
penalty is just the cost of spreading probability mass over a region the data never
visit. In the second case samples come from the wide distribution and are scored by the
narrow one: samples at $|x| = 3$ or more are three or more standard deviations out
under $q$, and $\log q$ punishes them quadratically. The direction in which samples come
from the *broader* distribution is the expensive one.

This asymmetry is the single most consequential fact about variational inference.
Mean-field VI minimises $\KL(q\,\|\,p)$ with the approximation $q$ in the first slot, so
$q$ is penalised for putting mass where $p$ has none, but barely penalised for missing
mass that $p$ has. The result is approximations that are too narrow. You will measure
this directly in Module 11.

The cleanest picture of the two behaviours is a single Gaussian fitted to a two-mode
target under each direction:

![A Gaussian $q$ fitted to a bimodal $p$ by minimising each KL direction. $\KL(q\,\|\,p)$ sits on one mode and ignores the other (mode-seeking, the variational choice). $\KL(p\,\|\,q)$ matches the moments and covers both modes with a wide Gaussian that puts most of its mass where $p$ has none (mass-covering).](../figures/m04_kl_bimodal.png){width=75%}

::: {.callout-note title="Interactive"}
The black curve is the bimodal target $p$; the orange curve is a Gaussian $q$ you control by dragging (left and right moves the mean, up and down changes the width) or with the sliders. The two readouts are $\KL(q\,\|\,p)$, which variational inference minimises, and $\KL(p\,\|\,q)$, which moment matching and maximum likelihood minimise. The lower panels draw the two integrands: $q\log(q/p)$ is large wherever $q$ puts mass that $p$ lacks, so the $\KL(q\,\|\,p)$ optimum sits inside one mode and is narrow; $p\log(p/q)$ is large wherever $p$ has mass that $q$ lacks, so the $\KL(p\,\|\,q)$ optimum straddles both modes and is wide. The two buttons animate $q$ to each optimum. Compare the widths.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="bi-widget" id="kl-direction" data-mu="0" data-sigma="1" style="width:100%;max-width:860px;margin:0 auto 1.5rem auto;"></div>
<script type="module">
```

Fitting the two-mode target is not a curiosity: a mixture posterior (Module 6), a
funnel (Module 11) and a multimodal likelihood all present exactly this choice, and
mean-field VI makes it the same way every time.

### The Bregman identity, line by line

Take two members $p = p(\cdot\mid\eta_p)$ and $q = p(\cdot\mid\eta_q)$ of one exponential
family with log-partition $A$. Substitute the exponential-family form into the
definition:

$$
\KL(p\,\|\,q) = \E_p\Big[\big(\log h(x) + \eta_p^\top t(x) - A(\eta_p)\big) - \big(\log h(x) + \eta_q^\top t(x) - A(\eta_q)\big)\Big].
$$

The base measure $\log h(x)$ cancels because it does not depend on $\eta$. What remains
is linear in $t(x)$ plus constants:

$$
\KL(p\,\|\,q) = (\eta_p - \eta_q)^\top\E_p[t(x)] - A(\eta_p) + A(\eta_q).
$$

Now use Module 3's identity $\E_p[t(x)] = \nabla A(\eta_p)$ and rearrange:

$$
\KL(p\,\|\,q) = A(\eta_q) - A(\eta_p) - (\eta_q - \eta_p)^\top\nabla A(\eta_p) = D_A(\eta_q, \eta_p).
$$

That is the Bregman divergence of $A$: the height of $A$ at $\eta_q$ above the tangent
plane drawn at $\eta_p$. Convexity of $A$ gives $\KL \ge 0$ a second time, now by a
picture rather than by Jensen.

![Left: the Bernoulli log-partition $A(\eta) = \log(1 + e^\eta)$, its tangent line at $\eta_p$ (conversion rate $6.2\%$), and the vertical gap at $\eta_q$ ($7.9\%$). The gap is $\KL(p\,\|\,q) = 0.00213$ nats; the inset zooms in because at these rates the curve is nearly straight. Right: the same tangent line extended to $\eta = 0$. Its slope is the mean parameter $\mu_p$ and its intercept is $-A^*(\mu_p)$, the entropy of $p$. The conjugate is a picture of a tangent line.](../figures/m04_bregman_tangent.png)

::: {.callout-note title="Interactive"}
The surface is the log-partition function $A(\eta) = \log(1 + e^{\eta_1} + e^{\eta_2})$ of a three-category Categorical. The blue plane is tangent to it at $\eta_p$; the red segment at $\eta_q$ runs from the plane up to the surface and its length is $D_A(\eta_q, \eta_p)$. The readout computes the same number as $\sum_k p_k\log(p_k/q_k)$; the two agree for every position of the sliders, and the segment never points downward because a convex surface lies above all its tangent planes. Press Play to let $\eta_q$ wander and watch the gap grow as $q$ moves away from $p$. The bars show the probability vectors $p$ and $q$ that the two natural-parameter points represent.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="bi-widget" id="bregman-surface" data-p1="-1" data-p2="0.5" data-q1="1.5" data-q2="-1" style="width:100%;max-width:860px;margin:0 auto 1.5rem auto;"></div>
```

The picture is the same in any dimension: a convex surface, a tangent plane, a
vertical gap. The interactive surface above shows it for a three-category Categorical,
where $\eta$ has two coordinates and the tangent plane is a real plane.

The practical consequence is that one function of `log_partition` and `mean_params`
yields every closed-form KL in the family table. The textbook formulas for the
Bernoulli, Categorical, Gamma and Dirichlet, which you will write by hand in Step 2, are
special cases, and the tests confirm they agree to ten digits.

### A worked example with numbers

The two landing-page variants of `ab_test_conversions` have true rates $p_A = 0.062$ and
$p_B = 0.079$. As Bernoulli natural parameters,
$\eta_A = \log\frac{0.062}{0.938} = -2.717$ and $\eta_B = \log\frac{0.079}{0.921} = -2.456$.
From Module 3, $A(\eta_A) = \log(1 + e^{\eta_A}) = 0.0640$,
$A(\eta_B) = 0.0823$, and $\nabla A(\eta_A) = p_A = 0.062$. The Bregman identity gives

$$
\KL(A\,\|\,B) = 0.0823 - 0.0640 - (-2.456 + 2.717)\times 0.062 = 0.00213 \text{ nats}.
$$

The textbook formula $p\log\frac{p}{q} + (1-p)\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}$ gives the same
$0.00213$, and the other direction is $\KL(B\,\|\,A) = 0.00230$. Both are tiny: a single
conversion event barely distinguishes a 6.2% rate from a 7.9% one. By the Chernoff–Stein
reading, telling the two apart at a 5% error rate needs about
$\log 20 / 0.00213 \approx 1400$ observations per arm. The experiment has about 400.
Module 5 will compute the posterior probability that B is better and find it close to
a coin flip; this calculation says in advance that it must.

### Dual coordinates: the Gaussian as the running example

A minimal exponential family has two natural coordinate systems. The Gaussian makes
them concrete:

| Coordinates | Univariate Gaussian | Role |
|---|---|---|
| natural $\eta$ | $(\mu/\sigma^2,\ -1/(2\sigma^2))$ | densities multiply by adding $\eta$ |
| mean $\mu$ | $(\E[x], \E[x^2]) = (\mu, \sigma^2 + \mu^2)$ | expectations and moment matching |

The map between them is $\mu(\eta) = \nabla A(\eta)$, and because $A$ is strictly convex
on a minimal family its gradient is one-to-one: every valid mean parameter corresponds to
exactly one natural parameter. For the Gaussian the inverse map is explicit
($\sigma^2 = \E[x^2] - \E[x]^2$, then $\eta$ from $\mu, \sigma^2$). For the Gamma and
Dirichlet it is not: inverting $(\psi(\alpha) - \log\beta, \alpha/\beta)$ for
$(\alpha, \beta)$ has no closed form. Step 3 solves it numerically.

### The convex conjugate and entropy

Go back to the right panel of the tangent-line figure. A convex curve can be described
two ways: by its height $A(\eta)$ at each point, or by the family of its tangent lines.
A tangent line is fixed by its slope and its intercept. The slope at $\eta$ is
$\mu = \nabla A(\eta)$, the mean parameter. The intercept, where the line crosses
$\eta = 0$, is $A(\eta) - \eta\,\nabla A(\eta) = A(\eta) - \eta\mu$. So "slope $\mu$,
intercept $A(\eta) - \eta\mu$" is a complete description of $A$ in mean coordinates. The
**convex conjugate** is minus that intercept as a function of the slope:

$$
A^*(\mu) = \eta(\mu)^\top\mu - A(\eta(\mu)),
$$

where $\eta(\mu)$ is the natural parameter whose mean parameter is $\mu$. The usual
definition, $A^*(\mu) = \sup_\eta\{\eta^\top\mu - A(\eta)\}$, says the same thing: for a
fixed slope $\mu$, slide a line of that slope until it just touches the curve, and read
off its intercept. Setting the gradient of the bracket to zero gives $\mu = \nabla A(\eta)$,
so the touching point is exactly $\eta(\mu)$. Because the curve is strictly convex, the
two descriptions determine each other: $\nabla A^* = (\nabla A)^{-1}$, and the Hessians
are inverse matrices, $\nabla^2 A^*(\mu) = F(\eta)^{-1}$. (If you have met the Legendre
transform in mechanics or thermodynamics, this is that construction; if not, the
tangent line is all you need.)

What is $A^*$? Compute the expected log density of a member with $\log h = 0$:

$$
\E_\eta[\log p(x\mid\eta)] = \eta^\top\E_\eta[t(x)] - A(\eta) = \eta^\top\mu - A(\eta) = A^*(\mu).
$$

The left side is $-H(p_\eta)$, the negative entropy. So the conjugate of the
log-partition function is the negative entropy expressed in mean coordinates. This is
why the entropy term of the ELBO in Module 6 is available in closed form for every
family here: it is $-A^*$, which you can evaluate through $A$.

### Newton's method, and why it needs damping

To find $\eta$ with $\nabla A(\eta) = \mu$, minimise $f(\eta) = A(\eta) - \eta^\top\mu$.
This is convex with gradient $\nabla A(\eta) - \mu$ and Hessian $F(\eta)$, so Newton's
method (Module 1, Step 3) is

$$
\eta \leftarrow \eta - F(\eta)^{-1}\big(\nabla A(\eta) - \mu\big).
$$

Near the solution it converges quadratically: the number of correct digits roughly
doubles per step. The problem is far from the solution. A Newton step is the minimiser
of a quadratic model of $f$, and the model knows nothing about $\Omega$. For the Gamma,
starting at $(\alpha, \beta) = (1, 1)$ and targeting $(3.5, 1.7)$, the first full step
pushes $\eta_2 = -\beta$ through zero. Outside $\Omega$ the normaliser does not exist,
$A$ returns `nan`, and every later iterate is `nan` too.

![Newton on the Gamma family in the natural-parameter plane. The domain is $\eta_2 < 0$. The full first step from $(0, -1)$ (red, dashed) crosses the boundary and every later iterate is `nan`. The damped path (orange) shortens the first step, stays inside, and converges quadratically to $(2.5, -1.7)$.](../figures/m04_newton_damping.png){width=65%}

The standard fix is a backtracking line search: try the full step, then half of it, then
a quarter, down to $2^{-10}$, and take the largest one for which $f$ is finite and does
not increase. Because $f$ is convex, some fraction of the Newton direction always
decreases it, so the search always succeeds while the iterate is inside $\Omega$. If
the step selection is done with `jnp.where` on a boolean mask rather than a Python `if`,
the whole solver stays a pure JAX function, and `jax.grad` can differentiate through it
with respect to $\mu$. The tests use exactly that to verify $\nabla A^* = \eta$.

### Why this matters later

- **Module 5.** The posterior update is addition in $\eta$; the posterior mean of $\mu$
  is a convex combination in mean coordinates. Both coordinate systems appear.
- **Module 6.** The ELBO for a conjugate model is a sum of KL terms between members of
  the families built here, plus entropies, all closed form via $A$ and $A^*$.
- **Module 8, Challenge; Module 6, Challenge.** The natural gradient of the ELBO
  (optional Step 4 below), which turns stochastic variational inference on a conjugate
  model into a running average of sufficient statistics.
- **Module 10.** HMC's mass matrix is the Fisher metric of the posterior in disguise:
  rescale coordinates so the posterior looks round.
- **Module 11 and Track A.** The under-dispersion of mean-field VI, predicted here from
  the asymmetry of KL, is measured against HMC and repaired with normalising flows.

### Common misconceptions

- **"KL is a distance."** It is asymmetric and violates the triangle inequality. The
  two directions answer different questions and can differ by a large factor.
- **"Minimising KL is the same whichever way round."** $\KL(q\,\|\,p)$ (variational
  inference) is mode-seeking and under-dispersed; $\KL(p\,\|\,q)$ (moment matching,
  expectation propagation, maximum likelihood) is mass-covering. Choosing the direction
  chooses the failure mode.
- **"Natural gradient is just preconditioning with any positive matrix."** It is
  preconditioning with the one matrix that makes the step invariant to how you
  parameterise the family. Change coordinates and the natural-gradient step changes
  covariantly; an arbitrary preconditioner does not.
- **"Newton always converges for convex problems."** Only with damping, and only from
  inside the domain. Convexity guarantees a descent direction, not that the full step
  stays feasible.

## Steps

Every step edits `workshop/m04_kl_bregman.py`. Import families from `.m03_expfam`.

### Step 1 — KL as a Bregman divergence

**What this computes.** The Bregman identity, generically: given any `ExpFam` and two
natural parameters, the KL divergence from `log_partition` and `mean_params` alone. The
Monte Carlo companion is the definition of KL applied literally: draw from $p$, average
$\log p - \log q$. Agreement between the two is the first test, and it is the pattern
of test you will use for every closed-form expectation in the workshop.

Implement `kl(fam, eta_p, eta_q)` as
`fam.log_partition(eta_q) - fam.log_partition(eta_p) - (eta_q - eta_p) @ fam.mean_params(eta_p)`.
Implement `kl_monte_carlo(fam, eta_p, eta_q, key, n)` drawing `n` samples from $p$ and
returning the mean and standard error of $\log p(x) - \log q(x)$.

Sanity check: `kl(Bernoulli(), to_natural(0.062), to_natural(0.079))` should print
`0.00213`, the number from the worked example.

```bash
pytest tests/m04 -k step1
```

You should see 4 passed: zero at equal arguments, positivity and asymmetry for Gamma,
agreement with your own Monte Carlo estimate for Gamma, Dirichlet and Categorical, and
agreement with `kl_gaussians` from Module 2 for a bivariate Gaussian.

### Step 2 — Textbook closed forms

**What this computes.** The same divergences, written in the parameters you would
report. Deriving them by hand from the Bregman form is the exercise: substitute the
family's $A$ and $\nabla A$ from the Module 3 table and simplify. The tests compare
your hand formulas to the generic `kl` at `rtol=1e-10`, so any algebra slip shows.

Implement `kl_bernoulli(p, q)`, `kl_categorical(p, q)`,
`kl_gamma(alpha_p, beta_p, alpha_q, beta_q)` and `kl_dirichlet(alpha_p, alpha_q)` from
their standard parameterisations. For the Gamma,

$$
\KL = (\alpha_p - \alpha_q)\psi(\alpha_p) - \log\Gamma(\alpha_p) + \log\Gamma(\alpha_q) + \alpha_q\log\tfrac{\beta_p}{\beta_q} + \alpha_p\tfrac{\beta_q - \beta_p}{\beta_p}.
$$

Sanity check: `kl_categorical(p, p)` is `0.0` for any `p`, and
`kl_bernoulli(0.062, 0.079)` matches Step 1.

```bash
pytest tests/m04 -k step2
```

You should see 4 passed, each comparing your formula against `kl` on the family at
`rtol=1e-10`.

### Step 3 — Inverting the mean map and the conjugate

**What this computes.** The map from mean parameters back to natural parameters, by
damped Newton on the convex objective $A(\eta) - \eta^\top\mu$, and then the conjugate
$A^*(\mu)$ and a Monte Carlo entropy to confirm $A^* = -H$. The differentiability test
checks the duality $\nabla A^* = \eta$ by running `jax.grad` through your solver.

Implement `natural_from_mean(fam, mu, eta0, n_iter=30)` as damped Newton: direction
$d = -F(\eta)^{-1}(\nabla A(\eta) - \mu)$, candidate steps $\eta + 2^{-k}d$ for
$k = 0, \dots, 10$ evaluated with `jax.vmap`, accept the first candidate with finite,
non-increasing objective using `jnp.argmax` on a boolean mask and `jnp.where`. Run
exactly `n_iter` iterations in `lax.fori_loop`.

Implement `conjugate(fam, mu, eta0)` as `eta @ mu - fam.log_partition(eta)` with
`eta = natural_from_mean(...)`, and `entropy_monte_carlo(fam, eta, key, n)`.

Sanity check: for the Gamma with $(\alpha, \beta) = (3.5, 1.7)$, take
`mu = fam.mean_params(eta)` and run `natural_from_mean(fam, mu, jnp.array([0., -1.]))`;
it should return `[2.5, -1.7]`. Try it without damping first to see the `nan`.

```bash
pytest tests/m04 -k step3
```

You should see 3 passed: round-trips `mean_params(natural_from_mean(mu)) = mu` for
Bernoulli, Categorical, Gamma and Dirichlet; $A^*(\mu) = -H$ for a Gamma against Monte
Carlo; and `jax.grad(conjugate)(mu) = eta` for a Dirichlet, differentiating through the
solver.

### Step 4 — Fisher metric and natural gradient (optional)

**What this computes.** The second-order expansion of KL and the natural gradient
$F^{-1}\nabla_\eta f$. The first test checks the expansion is second-order accurate (the
error must drop by about $1000\times$, at least $500\times$, when $\delta$ shrinks
tenfold). The second checks the identity natural gradient equals $\nabla_\mu f$ by
differentiating $f(\eta(\mu))$ through Step 3's solver. Nothing later in the required
path depends on this step; it is used by the Challenges of Modules 6 and 8. If you are
behind, read the derivation and come back.

**Steepest descent depends on the ruler.** Gradient descent takes the step that
decreases the loss most *per unit of parameter change*. But "unit of parameter change"
depends on coordinates. Move the Bernoulli natural parameter by $\delta\eta = 1$: at
$p = 0.5$ the distribution changes by $\KL = 0.120$ nats; at $p = 0.062$ the same step
changes it by only $0.039$ nats. The same parameter step is three times smaller as a
change in distribution. An optimiser that moves a fixed distance in $\eta$ is therefore
moving three times too cautiously at the low rate, or three times too aggressively at
the high one.

The fix is to measure parameter steps by how much they change the distribution. The
Bregman identity expanded to second order gives

$$
\KL(p_\eta\,\|\,p_{\eta+\delta}) = \tfrac12\delta^\top F(\eta)\delta + O(\|\delta\|^3),
$$

(check: at $p = 0.062$, $F = 0.0582$, and $\tfrac12 F \times 0.1^2 = 0.00029$ against the
exact $0.00030$ for $\delta = 0.1$.) So the Fisher matrix is the local ruler on
distribution space. Steepest descent with respect to this ruler replaces $\nabla_\eta f$
with

$$
\tilde\nabla f = F(\eta)^{-1}\nabla_\eta f,
$$

the **natural gradient**. For an exponential family there is a further simplification.
By the chain rule, $\nabla_\eta f = \frac{\partial\mu}{\partial\eta}^\top\nabla_\mu f = F\,\nabla_\mu f$,
so

$$
F^{-1}\nabla_\eta f = \nabla_\mu f:
$$

the natural gradient in natural coordinates is the ordinary gradient in mean
coordinates. The Challenges of Modules 6 and 8 use this: natural-gradient stochastic
VI on a conjugate model is a weighted average of expected sufficient statistics, with
no matrix inverse in sight.

Implement `natural_gradient(fam, eta, grad_eta)` as `solve(F(eta), grad_eta)` and
`kl_quadratic_approx(fam, eta, delta)` as $\frac12\delta^\top F\delta$.

Sanity check: `kl_quadratic_approx(Bernoulli(), to_natural(0.062), jnp.array([0.1]))`
should print `0.00029`, against `kl(...)` of `0.00030`.

```bash
pytest tests/m04 -k step4
```

You should see 2 passed: the quadratic approximation error shrinks by a factor of at
least 500 when $\delta$ shrinks tenfold (third-order remainder), and for a Categorical
the natural gradient equals $\nabla_\mu f$ computed by differentiating
$f(\eta(\mu))$ through `natural_from_mean`.

## Checkpoint

::: {.callout-tip title="Checkpoint"}
```bash
pytest tests/m04
```
13 tests pass (11 if you skipped Step 4). You now have closed-form KL and entropy for
every family, which is what makes the ELBO of Module 6 computable without sampling.
Before moving on, be able to say in one sentence each: why KL is asymmetric, what the
Bregman picture shows, and what a natural gradient corrects for.

**Which expectation did you just compute?** KL itself: $\E_p[\log p - \log q]$, an
expectation under the first argument. Step 1 computed it in closed form through $A$;
`kl_monte_carlo` computed the same expectation by sampling. Entropy is
$-\E_p[\log p]$, the special case $q$ uniform.
:::

## Challenge

::: {.callout-note title="Challenge"}
1. The reverse Bregman divergence $D_A(\eta_p, \eta_q)$ is $\KL(q\,\|\,p)$. Show that
   in mean coordinates $\KL(p\,\|\,q) = D_{A^*}(\mu_p, \mu_q)$ and verify numerically
   with your `conjugate`. Which of the two divergences does mean-field VI minimise,
   and what does that imply about the fitted variances?
2. Implement `natural_from_mean` for the over-complete Gaussian of Module 3 by
   working in the minimal coordinates of its Challenge 1, and confirm it agrees with
   the closed-form `to_natural(mu, Sigma)` recovered from the mean parameters
   $(\mu, \Sigma + \mu\mu^\top)$.
3. Run plain gradient descent and natural gradient descent on
   $f(\eta) = \KL(p_{\eta^*}\,\|\,p_\eta)$ for a Bernoulli with $p^* = 0.062$, starting
   from $p = 0.5$, with the same step size. Plot KL against iteration for both and explain
   the difference using the ruler argument.
:::

## Going deeper

- Wainwright and Jordan (2008), Sections 3.4–3.6 (mean parameters, the conjugate dual,
  and the variational representation of $A$) and Appendix B.
- MacKay, *Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms* (Cambridge University
  Press, 2003), Chapter 2 for the coding reading of KL and Chapter 8 for the testing
  reading. Short and concrete.
- Amari, *Information Geometry and Its Applications* (Springer, 2016), Chapters 1–2
  (dually flat structure of exponential families; Bregman divergences).
- Hoffman, Blei, Wang and Paisley, "Stochastic Variational Inference", *JMLR* 14 (2013),
  Section 2.3 for the natural gradient of the ELBO in a conjugate exponential family.
- Nielsen and Nock, "Entropies and cross-entropies of exponential families" (2010), for
  the entropy formula $H = A(\eta) - \eta^\top\nabla A(\eta) - \E[\log h]$.

## Troubleshooting

::: {.callout-warning title="Troubleshooting"}
**`natural_from_mean` returns `nan` for the Gamma.** Undamped Newton stepped out of
the domain. Confirm your candidate-step mask treats `nan` objective values as
unacceptable (`jnp.isfinite`) and that you fall back to the current iterate when no
candidate is acceptable.

**Round-trip passes but `jax.grad(conjugate)` fails.** You used a Python `if` or a
`while` loop in the line search, which breaks the trace, or `lax.while_loop`, which
is not reverse-mode differentiable. Use `lax.fori_loop` with a fixed count and
`jnp.where`.

**`kl_gamma` disagrees in the fourth decimal.** Mixed up shape/rate with
shape/scale, or used $\log\Gamma$ where $\psi$ (digamma) belongs.

**The quadratic-approximation test fails the ratio check.** You compared absolute
errors at one scale only; the test requires the error to drop by $\ge 500\times$ for
a $10\times$ smaller $\delta$. A factor of $100$ indicates you are missing the
$\frac12$ and the approximation is only first-order accurate.

**Your `kl` has the right magnitude but the wrong sign of asymmetry.** You evaluated the
tangent at $\eta_q$ instead of $\eta_p$. The expectation in KL is under the first
argument, so the mean parameters come from `eta_p`.

**You expected the Monte Carlo KL to be exactly non-negative.** The estimator is
unbiased but noisy; for nearly equal distributions it can come out slightly negative.
The closed form is always $\ge 0$; the sample estimate is $\ge 0$ only in expectation.
:::
